title_original: Opinion: As Federal Support for Culture Falls, We Need a New Generation of Giving
editorial_title_zh: 观点：随着联邦对文化的资助减少，我们需要新一代的捐赠
editorial_excerpt_zh: "我们花了如此长的时间去讨好少数人，以至于几乎忘记了如何邀请大众——而这正是我们现在要做的工作。"

"text": "我在底特律郊区长大，我热爱的第一家博物馆是底特律艺术学院。甚至在我知道博物馆是做什么用之前，我就已经熟悉了这栋建筑及其珍宝：环绕中庭的迭戈·里韦拉（Diego Rivera）壁画，文森特·梵高（Vincent van Gogh）的自画像——这是他的作品中第一幅进入美国公共收藏的作品。我以一种属于孩子的笃定明白，某个重要的事情在那里发生，而我有幸能置身其旁。多年后，当底特律市遭遇美国历史上最大规模的市政府破产危机时，那栋建筑里的艺术品几乎要被变卖来偿还债权人的债务。那些伴随我长大的杰作被列入清单并标上了价格。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "拯救它们的既不是市场，也不是华盛顿特区。而是一个由基金会、州政府以及至关重要的博物馆自身捐赠者组成的联盟，他们共同凑集了大约8.16亿美元，既保持了藏品的完整，同时也保护了城市工人的养老金。他们共同决定，这种文化值得保留。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "某种版本的决定现在就摆在我们所有人面前。过去一年里，联邦政府采取行动逐步拆除对艺术和文化的资助。取消国家艺术基金会、国家人文基金会以及博物馆和图书馆服务研究所的提议并未得逞；国会以大致先前的水平为这三家机构提供了资金。但纸面上存续的资金并不等同于真正到账的资金。已经在推进中的赠款被取消，员工被削减，而发放资助的机器在行项目保持不变的同时已被掏空。2025年的一项针对博物馆馆长的全国调查发现，三分之一的美国博物馆的政府资助或合同被取消，其中三分之二的博物馆根本没有补上这笔资金。行政部门已再次提议将这三个机构的预算清零。各机构无法据此进行规划，而规划正是全部的工作。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "梅隆基金会（Mellon）、福特基金会（Ford）等各大基金会已经明确表示，它们无法替代政府撤出的资金。因此，我们的文化必须依靠私人捐赠来向前推进。问题在于哪种类型的捐赠：来自顶层、改变机构命运的大笔捐赠，还是来自更多普通人的更广泛的捐赠基础——他们或许永远不会为某个侧楼捐款，但他们的参与使得文化无论如何都值得捍卫。几十年来，艺术界在培养前者方面变得异常出色，但我无法停止思考的是后者，以及如果这种努力失败，文化将会面临怎样的命运。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "广泛的基础是未来主要捐赠者应当涌现的地方，但美国家庭向慈善机构捐款的比例多年来一直在下降，尽管美国人捐赠的总额有所增长。而这个基础在某人开出大额支票的很久之前就已经建立起来了。它始于人们获得接触文化的机会、与文化建立联系，并开始相信自己对文化的命运负有一定的责任。我们花了如此长的时间去讨好少数人，以至于几乎忘记了如何邀请大众——而这正是我们现在要做的工作。", "translated": "慈善拍卖给慈善事业的其他领域上了一课，而这一课常常被遗忘：人们的捐赠并非出于计算，而是出于情感。没有人是为了填补预算缺口而举起拍卖牌的——他们举牌是为了让孩子的脸上露出笑容，或者为了影响他们能够想象改变的一件事。我在现场募款那5分钟里的全部工作，就是让一个原本有所戒备的房间去想象那件事，直到他们感同身受。我曾见过三位陌生人在听到单一的呼吁后各自承诺捐赠5万美元，事前没有任何托儿或预先安排。这项事业不再是一个抽象概念，而第一个迈出这一步的人的勇气赋予了其他人效仿的许可。无论捐款是50美元还是5000万美元，道理都是一样的。", Foundation）——在那里你了解到掌声熄灭很久之后金钱的去向。但无论从哪个角度来看，争取支持最难的部分是塑造捐赠者与事业之间的情感联系。正因如此，当我离开拍卖行业创立自己的公司时，我发现：我在那里指导收藏家建立战后及当代艺术收藏，并就能够赋予这些收藏超越墙面之意义的慈善事业向他们提供建议。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "当收藏家开始将藏品视为一种慈善工具时——无论是将作品借给展览、构建捐赠结构，还是支持使收藏成为可能的机构和艺术家——收藏和捐赠就不再是两个独立的决定。碰巧的是，这里有一个代际特征：把一个想法带给年轻收藏家，答案往往是肯定的，因为他们仍在建设中；而把它带给年长的收藏家，答案往往是否定的，因为他们觉得已经被榨干了底气。", "translated": true}, {"type": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "那么，我们该如何把所有人凝聚在一起？这不会靠更好的税收论点，而是靠我们调动现场氛围的方式。我们需要降低门槛，让人们感觉自己属于文化内部，而不是局外人、仅仅在开支票。这一切始于准入——艺术家们正在以身作则。在她的近期展览（于玛丽安·古德曼画廊举办）最后一场舞蹈演出后的晚宴上，朱莉·梅赫雷图（Julie Mehretu）向我讲述了她在工作室创作之外所协助创立的事业：卡茨基尔山的一处驻留项目、一个泛非电影倡议，以及最让我铭记于心的一件事——向惠特尼美术馆捐赠超过200万美元，让所有25岁以下的人都可以免费入场。梅赫雷图花的是她自己的钱——不是为了建一座冠以她名字的展厅，而是为了拆除那道常常阻隔在年轻人与艺术之间的唯一障壁。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "我的家乡曾在大规模上做到这一点，而时机的重要性远超我最初的理解。2012年，即该市申请破产的前一年，底特律大都会区的选民一致同意对自身加税以支持底特律艺术学院，以此换取居民免费入场以及为当地学校扩大准入。等到债权人为了艺术品蜂拥而至时，该地区早已认定这座博物馆属于他们自己。2020年，他们投票续签了这项立法，其支持率甚至比第一次时更高。这就是自下而上的引擎化为现实，而这种集体推动力在随后的救援中究竟起了多大作用，很值得我们深思。", "translated": true}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://www.artnews.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/dia.orgcollectionself-portrait46065.jpg?w=400", "alt": "戴着草帽的留须男子油画。", "caption": "我认识的最严肃的收藏家之一，几乎将其全部捐赠都给到了朋友们带他接触的事业，这是一种常见的机制，却也是一个潜在的陷阱，因为仅仅由朋友拉朋友画出的圈子，最终转来转去总是那些面孔。引导一个原本不在现场的人去刻意欣赏艺术，能够打破封闭的循环，这也是为什么你所做的一次引荐可能和一张支票同样重要。如果没有那些默默从事耐心且不那么光鲜的工作、一个关系一个关系地建立群众基础的人，这一切都无法存活。我们总是更乐于资助一个冠名的画廊，而不是那些兑现使命的薪酬，仿佛从事这些工作的人只是管理成本，而非引擎本身。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "我想到了米斯蒂·科普兰（Misty Copeland）。在我在美国芭蕾舞剧院的晚会上担任拍卖师之前，我并不知道她直到13岁才开始跳舞。如今，通过她的基金会，她正在为资源匮乏社区的儿童扩大接触舞蹈和芭蕾的机会，创造着让另一个孩子获得与她当年同样机遇的可能。她的慈善事业并非预算表上的一行字，而是对谁能参与、谁能被看见、以及最终是谁来塑造下一代文化的投资。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "如果说美国生活的哪个角落能够将顶层的资本与底层的群众连结起来，并让捐赠感觉像是一种归属而非一种义务，那就是艺术界。我们拥有收藏家、带头前行的艺术家、承载记忆的机构，以及其他任何领域都无法等量齐观的一样东西：在一处空间里让人们共同感受到某种真实事物的力量。长期以来，我们一直将自己视为一个市场、一场地位游戏、少数人的避难所。而我们本可以成为这个国家最具力量的文化与慈善空间之一，因为我们已经具备了所需的一切。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "底特律艺术学院的藏品部分是由几家基金会拯救的。但这座博物馆如今属于它的城市，是因为整个地区的普通老百姓投票宣布它是他们自己的。这就是全部的答案：底层与顶层共同决定某样东西值得保留。剩下的唯一问题是，我们当中会有多少人作出同样的决定，而当我们这样做时，又会各自带上多少其他人。", "translated": true}]

But the money surviving on paper is not the same as the money arriving. Grants already in motion were canceled, staff were cut, and the machinery that delivers the funding was hollowed out while the line items stayed intact. So it is private giving that will have to carry our culture forward. For a generation, the art world has become extraordinarily good at cultivating the first, but what I cannot stop thinking about is the second, and what becomes of a culture if it fails."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "The broad base is where tomorrow’s major donors need to come from, but the share of American households giving to charity has been declining for years, even as the total amount Americans give has grown. I have spent my career watching both. I started in the art world at an auction house, where I trained as an auctioneer and learned how the market moves and what makes a serious collector decide to bid. Over time, I started being asked to serve as a benefit auctioneer, and have since raised more than $50 million that way—for museums and foundations, dance companies and cultural nonprofits, parks and schools, preservation campaigns and health clinics. My whole job in the five minutes of a live ask is to make a guarded room imagine that one thing until they feel it. I have watched three strangers each pledge $50,000 in response to a single ask, with no plant and nothing prearranged. The cause stopped being an abstraction, and the courage of the one who went first gave the others permission to follow. article_text:
Kimberly Pirtle is the founder of Gabriel Advisory Group, an art advisory and philanthropy advisory firm working with collectors and institutions. Previously, she worked at Sotheby’s.

I grew up in the suburbs of Detroit, and the first museum I loved was the Detroit Institute of Arts. Before I even knew what a museum was for, I knew the building and its treasures: the Diego Rivera murals wrapping the courtyard, the Vincent van Gogh self-portrait that was the first of his works to enter an American public collection. I understood, with a child’s certainty, that something important happened there and that I was allowed to be near it. Years later, when the city of Detroit went bankrupt in the largest municipal failure in American history, the art inside that building was nearly sold off to pay the city’s creditors. The masterpieces I had grown up walking past were put on a list and given a price.

What saved them was neither the market nor Washington, D.C. It was a coalition of foundations, the state, and, crucially, the museum’s own donors who collectively put up roughly $816 million to keep the collection whole and protect the city workers’ pensions at the same time. They decided, together, that the culture was worth keeping.

Some version of that decision now sits in front of all of us. Over the past year, the federal government has moved to dismantle its support for arts and culture. The proposals to eliminate the National Endowment for the Arts, the National Endowment for the Humanities, and the Institute of Museum and Library Services have not succeeded; Congress funded all three at roughly their prior levels. But the money surviving on paper is not the same as the money arriving. Grants already in motion were canceled, staff were cut, and the machinery that delivers the funding was hollowed out while the line items stayed intact. A 2025 national survey of museum directors found that one-third of American museums had government grants or contracts canceled, and two-thirds of those museums have not replaced the money at all. The administration has proposed zeroing out all three agencies again. The institutions cannot plan against that, and planning is the whole job.

Great foundations like Mellon, Ford, and their peers have said plainly that they cannot replace what the government is withdrawing. So it is private giving that will have to carry our culture forward. The question is which kind: institution-changing gifts from the top, or a broader base of giving from people who may never endow a wing but whose participation makes culture worth defending at all. For a generation, the art world has become extraordinarily good at cultivating the first, but what I cannot stop thinking about is the second, and what becomes of a culture if it fails.

The broad base is where tomorrow’s major donors need to come from, but the share of American households giving to charity has been declining for years, even as the total amount Americans give has grown. And that base is built long before someone writes a major check. It begins when people are given access to culture, develop a relationship to it, and come to believe that they have some responsibility for what happens to it. We have spent so long courting the few that we have half forgotten how to invite the many—and that is the work now.

TOP-DOWN AND BOTTOM-UP ways of giving are different engines that do different kinds of work. I have spent my career watching both. I started in the art world at an auction house, where I trained as an auctioneer and learned how the market moves and what makes a serious collector decide to bid. Over time, I started being asked to serve as a benefit auctioneer, and have since raised more than $50 million that way—for museums and foundations, dance companies and cultural nonprofits, parks and schools, preservation campaigns and health clinics. The list goes on.

Charity auctions teach a lesson that the rest of philanthropy often forgets: People do not give from calculation—they give from feeling. No one raises a paddle to fill a budget gap—they raise it to put a smile on the face of a child, or to affect one thing they can picture changing. My whole job in the five minutes of a live ask is to make a guarded room imagine that one thing until they feel it. I have watched three strangers each pledge $50,000 in response to a single ask, with no plant and nothing prearranged. The cause stopped being an abstraction, and the courage of the one who went first gave the others permission to follow. That works the same whether the gift is $50 or $50 million.

I see the other side of it with the boards I sit on—in the world of dance, at A.I.M. by Kyle Abraham, and in civic life, at the Governors Island Foundation—where you learn what becomes of the money long after the applause. But, from any vantage, the hardest part of earning support is shaping the emotional connection a giver has to the cause. That is what I discovered when I left the auction world to create my own firm, where I guide collectors in building collections of postwar and contemporary art and advise them on the philanthropy that can give those collections a purpose beyond the wall.

Collecting and giving cease being two separate decisions when a collector begins to see a collection as a philanthropic instrument—whether by lending a work to an exhibition, structuring a gift, or supporting the institutions and artists that made the collection possible. And, as it happens, there is a generational tell in it: Bring an idea to a younger collector and the answer is often yes, because they are still building; bring it to an older one and it is often no, because they feel tapped.

The art world frets endlessly over how to get young people to collect and less over how to get them to give, which is backward. The appetite is there. Millennials now coming into real money are caught between two extremes: more power than any generation in memory to decide what survives, and grief for the loss of the more felt and humane culture of their own childhoods. That grief is not a weakness. It is an opening.

So how do we bring everyone along? It won’t be with a better tax argument but with the way we move a room. We need to lower the barrier and let people feel they belong inside the culture rather than outside it, just writing checks. It begins with access—and artists are showing how. Over dinner after the final dance performance of her recent show, staged at Marian Goodman Gallery, Julie Mehretu told me what she helped create away from her work in her studio: a residency in the Catskills, a pan-African film initiative, and—the thing that stayed with me most—a donation of more than $2 million to the Whitney Museum, so that anyone under 25 years old gets in free. Mehretu spent her own money—not on a wing with her name on it but on removing what’s often the one barrier between a young person and art.

My hometown did that at scale, and the timing matters more than I understood at first. In 2012, a year before the city filed for bankruptcy, voters across metro Detroit agreed to tax themselves to support the DIA in exchange for free admission for residents and expanded access for local schools. By the time the creditors came for the art, the region had already decided the museum was theirs. In 2020 they voted to renew the legislation, by wider margins than the first time. That is the bottom-up engine made real, and it is worth considering how much the collective push had to do with the rescue that followed.

ONE OF THE MOST SERIOUS collectors I know gives almost entirely to the causes his friends bring him into, which is a common mechanism but also a potential trap, because a circle drawn only by friends inviting friends keeps turning up the same faces. Taking someone on the journey of appreciating art deliberately, someone who wasn’t already in the room, can widen a closed loop, which is why an introduction you make can matter as much as a check. And none of it survives without the people who do the patient, unglamorous work of building a base one relationship at a time. We are quicker to fund a named gallery than the salaries that deliver the mission, as if the people doing the work were overhead rather than the engine itself.

I think of Misty Copeland, who, until I auctioneered at a gala for American Ballet Theatre, I did not realize had only begun dancing at 13. Today, through her foundation, she is expanding access to dance and ballet for children in under-resourced communities, creating the possibility that another child might be given the same chance she was. Her philanthropy is not a line in a budget. It is an investment in who gets to participate, who gets to be seen, and, ultimately, who gets to shape the culture next.

If any corner of American life can connect the capital at the top to the base at the bottom and make giving feel like belonging rather than a duty, it is the art world. We have the collectors, the artists already leading, the institutions that hold the memory, and the one thing no other field has in the same measure: the power to make people feel something true in a room together. We have long thought of ourselves as a market, a status game, a refuge for the few. We could instead be one of the country’s most powerful spaces for culture and philanthropy, because we already have everything it takes.

The collection of the Detroit Institute of Arts was saved in part by a few foundations. But the museum now belongs to its city because a whole region of ordinary people voted to call it their own. That is the entire answer: the top and the bottom deciding together that something is worth keeping. The only question left is how many of us will decide the same, and how many others we each bring along when we do.

article_text:
Following an initial announcement in June , Skulptur Projekte Münster has revealed 13 additional artists and groups that will be contributing site-specific commissions to its sixth edition. The exhibition, led by the curatorial collective What, How & for Whom (WHW), will take place from 13 June to 3 October.

The newly announced artists are: Mercedes Azpilicueta, Nolan Oswald Dennis , Alice Creischer and Andreas Siekmann, Myvillages, Kosen Ohtsubo, Kapwani Kiwanga, Iman Issa , Natascha Sadr Haghighian , Ashfika Rahman, Vlatka Horvat , Anton Kats, Khalil Rabah, Ali Cherri .

‘In times when cancellations, censorship, and withdrawal have constrained cultural work, Skulptur Projekte seeks to make room for voices to be heard, for losses to be mourned, for consolation, and for alternatives to be proposed’, WHW said in a statement.

‘An artwork in the public space need not compete for visibility in an already overly saturated world; it can offer time to witness, to feel, and to stay with what cannot readily be resolved. At a moment when political and economic propositions struggle to make a positive future imaginable, the faint hope of Skulptur Projekte 2027 is that such encounters with art in public space might allow for perspectives to be felt and acknowledged that are often misrepresented or obscured, without forcing consensus where none exists.’

article_text:
In 1983, Richard Gere was one of cinema’s hottest heartthrobs thanks to a string of sexually-charged roles in skillfully-executed star vehicles. After gaining traction in Hollywood with a sleazy supporting role in “Looking for Mr. Goodbar” and a riveting lead performance in Terrence Malick’s “ Days of Heaven ,” Gere became a star in Paul Schrader ‘s huge hit “American Gigolo,” then followed it with the even huger hit “An Officer and a Gentleman.”

“An Officer and a Gentleman” was an out-and-out phenomenon, outgrossed in 1982 only by “E.T.” and “Tootsie,” and if Gere’s follow-up, a lurid remake of Jean-Luc Godard’s “Breathless,” made considerably less money, it was still a hit — and a hit for which Gere could take most of the credit, since most critics didn’t seem to think there was much to the movie beyond Gere and co-star Valerie Kaprisky’s naked bodies. (In recent years, the movie has experienced a deserved reappraisal, largely motivated by the cheerleading of its most famous fan, Quentin Tarantino.)

Gere’s hot streak ended when he followed “Breathless” with “ The Honorary Consul ,” an adaptation of Graham Greene’s 1973 novel that failed at the box office, in spite of Paramount’s best efforts to trick audiences into thinking it was another ode to Gere’s sexuality rather than the thoughtful study in political intrigue that it actually was. For the U.S. audience, the movie was retitled “ Beyond the Limit ,” and Paramount created a poster depicting Gere in bed with a gorgeous woman looming over him in imagery echoing that of the recently released “Breathless.”

That imagery wasn’t exactly a lie — there are sex scenes between Gere’s character Eduardo Plarr and his friend Charley Fortnum’s (Michael Caine) young and beautiful wife Clara (Elpidia Carrillo) — but the poster failed to convey what “The Honorary Consul” was really about. As is typical of Greene’s work, it’s a tale of thorny moral issues, following the love triangle between an honorary British consul in Argentina, his ex-prostitute wife, and a brooding doctor, and examining the repercussions of that triangle when the consul is mistakenly kidnapped by a revolutionary who thinks the consul is the American ambassador.

Paramount’s bait-and-switch marketing was a disaster; straight women and gay men who came to the movie for a look at Gere’s firm rump weren’t happy to find so many scenes involving radicals being tortured in bathtubs filled with feces — and viewers who might have been interested in the film ‘s sophisticated moral arguments assumed it was just a mindless piece of soft-core pornography. Thus “The Honorary Consul,” aka “Beyond the Limit,” died at the box office, was excoriated by critics (including Greene himself, who hated Gere’s casting), and slid into obscurity almost immediately.

The movie deserved better, but for years it wasn’t even available for reconsideration — as far as I’ve been able to tell, there was never a U.S. physical media release beyond the initial VHS pressing, and even in Greene and director John Mackenzie ‘s native United Kingdom it didn’t come out until 2019. Now, however, the Australian label Imprint has issued an all-region Blu-ray release of the film as part of its “Directed by John Mackenzie” boxed set, a collection that would be worth purchasing for “The Honorary Consul” alone but which happens to contain a few other terrific movies as well.

Mackenzie’s a somewhat underrated figure, a Scottish filmmaker who worked with Ken Loach as an assistant director before embarking on his own career making similar works of social realism for British film and television. He’s best known today for his 1981 feature “The Long Good Friday,” a thriller about a scrappy criminal (Bob Hoskins in his first great film role) having the worst day of his life. Mackenzie beautifully captures London in the early days of Thatcher and uses the setting to both define and deepen the film’s ambitious and doomed protagonist; it’s a movie that honors Loach’s political tradition but infuses it with violent intensity and genre movie kicks.

“The Long Good Friday” is in the Imprint box along with two films Mackenzie made after “The Honorary Consul,” the Cold War thriller “The Fourth Protocol” and the cheeky JFK conspiracy flick “Ruby.” All four movies exhibit Mackenzie’s knack for trenchant social and political commentary slightly heightened by his elegance as a dramatist and visceral genre filmmaker, and all are accompanied by illuminating supplements.

“The Honorary Consul” is the real gem of the package though, as the collection’s most obscure and underrated release and the one most in need of the kind of context this set provides. The Blu-ray contains interviews with several key crew members who detail the film’s history and its problems, and there’s a terrific audio commentary by writer Matthew Asprey Gear, who delves into not only the making of “The Honorary Consul” but the aborted attempts at adaptation that preceded it.

Most fascinating among these is a proposed version to be directed by Orson Welles, who had played one of his most memorable roles in the Greene-scripted “The Third Man.” In a nod to that film, Welles and co-writer Oja Kodar called their screenplay adaptation of “The Honorary Consul” “The Other Man,” and it’s intriguing to consider Welles in the Michael Caine role, and to ponder how the story would have fit into his oeuvre of films about betrayal and power.

When Welles’ option lapsed in 1978, producer Norma Heyman (mother of future “Harry Potter” and “Once Upon a Time…in Hollywood” producer David Heyman) snapped up the rights and hired playwright Christopher Hampton to pen a new screenplay. Hampton was well positioned to write about Englishmen out of their element in a foreign country, having bounced around Egypt, Yemen, and Hong Kong when he was younger, and his 1973 play “Savages” shared a number of elements with Greene’s novel — though the similarities had to be coincidental given that “The Honorary Consul” came out the same year.

Hampton clearly had a knack for adapting British literary works, particularly those with political or espionage elements; he wrote multiple adaptations of Joseph Conrad’s books (including an adaptation of “Nostromo” for David Lean that was never filmed) and would return to Graham Greene for the 2002 version of “The Quiet American” — which, like “The Honorary Consul,” stars Michael Caine as the older man in a love triangle with a younger man and younger woman. Hampton’s script for “The Honorary Consul” skillfully distills the complexities of Greene’s novel into an efficient, beautifully paced drama that expertly juggles the criss-crossing characters and their shifting allegiances.

The script was strong enough to attract Gere and Caine, as well as Mackenzie’s “Long Good Friday” star Bob Hoskins, who is terrific in “Consul” as an insidious local police chief. Hoskins’ performances for Mackenzie are something special; the director knew how to exploit the actor’s natural amiability by having him play sinister characters whose violent tendencies are given more impact by the infectious smile that cloaks inner cruelty. Caine, of course, is excellent as usual, bringing a combination of resignation and dignity to the well-intentioned loser that he plays.

Caine’s performance was widely praised even by critics who didn’t care for the movie, like Roger Ebert. The same can’t be said for Gere, who was, admittedly, miscast in several ways. First off, the character in the book is weary and troubled, qualities Gere plays but which are offset by his natural confidence and charisma. More problematic was the character’s heritage; he’s supposed to be half-English and half-Paraguayan, and to say Gere’s accent is inconsistent would be charitable. Graham Greene disowned the movie, largely based on what he saw as Gere’s unsuitability for the part.

While I can’t entirely argue with the criticisms, I do think they fail to take into account the genuine strengths of Gere’s performance as Eduardo Plarr. He’s another of Gere’s chilly, unlikable characters, a trend that began with the ruthless opportunism of the fugitive farmhand in “Days of Heaven” and continued in “American Gigolo” and “Breathless.” The men in these films are so self-interested as to become almost sociopathic, though Julian Kay in “Gigolo” does have a last-minute moment of redemption (motivated less by anything in the actual plot than by Paul Schrader’s desire to remake “Pickpocket”).

Even Gere’s most overtly romantic lead role in “An Officer and a Gentleman,” the movie that solidified his status as a megastar, is often thuggish and unpleasant — Gere was never a movie star interested in begging for the audience’s approval. This is what made him interesting, and it’s what made him right for Plarr in spite of his struggles with the accent. Plarr is intentionally unreadable and unsympathetic, cold and uncaring about both his friend and the friend’s wife he is sleeping with, and Gere’s brooding self-absorption fits him perfectly.

It also stands in compelling relief against Michael Caine’s warm, engaging alcoholic rival for Clara’s affections; the scenes between the two men crackle with the tension that comes from seeing two equally powerful but stylistically opposite screen presences in collision. Greene purists, as well as the author himself, bristled at the way Gere’s casting transformed the story, but as pure drama the movie is riveting — and a fascinating case study in just how much a star persona can affect a film. Had Hoskins and Gere switched roles, for example, the movie would completely work without a single line of dialogue changed — it would be equally viable, and completely different.

Interestingly, the actor Mackenzie was initially concerned about was Michael Caine, who he thought of as too classy to play the drunken Fortnum. Caine quickly won Mackenzie over, however, and the director worked with him again on “The Fourth Protocol” and “Quicksand.” As for Gere, Mackenzie cast him before “An Officer and a Gentleman” came out, and when it was released during production the film’s success caused no end of headaches, as the studio was suddenly much more interested in Mackenzie’s film than it had been before, and the interference became the bane of Mackenzie’s existence.

Like most people, the director himself didn’t have many positive things to say about “The Honorary Consul” after the experience was behind him, and according to an interview on the Imprint disc with one of the movie’s editors, Mackenzie even stepped away from the picture for a while during postproduction. Bad reviews, studio interference, and a disgruntled author aside, however, “The Honorary Consul” remains a compelling entry in Mackenzie, Gere, and Caine’s filmographies, and its revived availability thanks to Imprint provides a welcome opportunity to discover its pleasures.

“The Honorary Consul” is available on Blu-ray as part of the “Directed by John Mackenzie” boxed set, now available from Imprint .
excerpt_original: "The Honorary Consul" ended the actor's hot streak at the box office in 1983 and vanished into obscurity, but a new physical media collection devoted to its director reveals it to be worthy of reappraisal.

article_text:
「坊や よい子だ ねんねしな」のオープニングも、「くまの子 みていた かくれんぼ」のエンディングも、歌詞を見ただけで映像が目に浮かび、思わず口ずさんでしまう人も多いのではないでしょうか。国民的アニメ「まんが日本昔ばなし」の50周年を記念したイベントが、麻布台ヒルズギャラリースペース（東京都港区虎ノ門）で10月25日（日）まで開かれています。

「まんが日本昔ばなし」は1975年に始まり、世代を超えて愛され続けてきました。市原悦子さん、常田富士男さんの温かな語りも印象的で、1470もの物語が放送されたそうです。会場の入り口には「にんげんっていいな」のフォトスポットが設けられ、1.8メートルの「にんげん」が出迎えてくれます。アニメーションの原画などが展示されているほか、ダイジェストの映像も鑑賞できます。

注目は、50周年を記念した史上最大規模のグッズ販売で、オープニングやエンディングのシーンをデザインした巾着袋やぬいぐるみ、チャームなどがそろいます。

また、隣接する麻布台ヒルズギャラリーカフェでは、「おむすびころりん」の世界観から着想を得た「欲張りじいさんのよくばりおにぎりセット」（1,320円、1日30食限定）や、「笠地蔵の黒胡麻ミルクラテ」（1,180円）などのコラボメニューも扱っています。カフェの営業は午前10時から午後8時まで（ラストオーダーは食事が午後7時、ドリンクが午後7時30分）。

POP UP BOX「まんが日本昔ばなし展―昔、むかし、あるところに…」は10月25日（日）まで、午前11時～午後7時30分。麻布台ヒルズギャラリースペース（麻布台ヒルズガーデンプラザA地下1階、地下鉄日比谷線・神谷町駅直結）。入場無料。詳しくは 特設ウェブサイト で。

article_text:
There were more new 4K restorations released in 2025 than I, or anyone, could ever hope to see. As such, it’s important to note that this list is limited to both what screened in New York City, where I live, and what I was able to catch. In my viewing I tended to prioritize projects that honored the original projection format of the movie (most often celluloid), and films that were fiercely independent, international, transgressive, or rarely screened. That said, I believe that everything on my list is truly deserving of a new audience, and that the work of the organizations and individuals behind these restorations is nothing short of heroic.

Greaser’s Palace (Robert Downey Sr., 1972) and Sticks and Bones (Robert Downey Sr., 1973)

Anthology Film Archives presented two of the most important restorations of this year, both films by the late, great Downey Sr. The work done on his surrealist western Greaser’s Palace was reportedly a seven-year effort—it took longer than expected to get the color right—that had been initiated after the original 35mm negative was miraculously rediscovered in 2017. A new 35mm print of that restoration premiered at Anthology this past October.

On the other end of the spectrum, Downey’s Sticks and Bones , a made-for-TV project commissioned by CBS, was long thought to exist only in a version with burned-in timecodes. When a 2” master videotape belonging to cinematographer Peter Powell was discovered, Anthology was able to preserve and present the film in a series devoted to Downey Sr.’s mid-career work. Made-for-TV films, which often have complicated rights issues and/or missing materials, are highly at risk, and each one that is preserved and restored is worthy of celebration.

Mortu nega (Flora Gomes, 1988)

Gomes’s debut feature, a structurally invigorating meditation on revolution, was restored as part of the African Film Heritage Project. The initiative, created by The Film Foundation’s World Cinema Project, the Pan-African Federation of Filmmakers, and UNESCO, in collaboration with Cineteca di Bologna, continues to bring lost masterpieces—an overused term that I don’t employ lightly—back to life. That metaphor is especially apt here, as the English translation for Mortu nega is Those Whom Death Refused .

Memory Lane (John M. Stahl, 1926)

In her introduction to Stahl’s comedic and tragic love triangle at the Museum of Modern Art’s annual Silent Movie Week, the Library of Congress’s Rachael Stoeltje very matter-of-factly explained that the new 35mm print that was being projected will last for 700 to 900 years if stored properly.

Dying (Michael Roemer, 1976)

Commissioned by Boston’s public television station WGBH, this poignant and candid documentary by Roemer—who passed away this year at the age of 97—offers the points of view of those in the process of dying of terminal illnesses. Now that the original 16mm print of his film has been restored in 4K thanks to The Film Desk, it will be able to reach many more people than it did upon release.

Black Girl (Ossie Davis, 1972)

Davis’s film about a young Black woman with dreams of escaping poverty and becoming a dancer, based on the hugely successful stage play written by J.E. Franklin, played three times at this year’s New York Film Festival, and each screening was sold out. It was presented on a new 35mm print, thanks to the dedicated work of the UCLA Film & Television Archive.

Will (Jessie Maple, 1981)

The debut feature by Maple, the first Black woman to join New York’s camera operators union, was an independent production shot on 16mm with a budget of $12,000. This compassionate study of addiction and recovery originally screened independently in community centers, churches, and educational institutions thanks to LJ Film Productions, the company Maple operated in collaboration with her husband, Leroy Patton. It has since been preserved by Indiana University’s Black Film Center & Archive.

Shock Video (Ken Camp, 1985)

This year, EZTV—an LA-based production co-op and ahead-of-its-time “microcinema” that started offering weekly programming in the early 1980s—was celebrated with retrospectives in New York and Los Angeles. As part of these programs, Elizabeth Purchell’s Muscle Distribution, a distributor of “scrappy, misfit films that don’t fit into any particular box,” independently restored the works of the pioneering queer filmmaker Ken Camp, including Shock Video , an intense and incredibly dark 12-minute trailer of sorts for an unfinished Super-8 horror feature called After the Comet .

The Arch (T’ang Shushuen, 1968)

For her self-financed debut feature, T’ang collaborated with Les Blank (who co-edited) and Subrata Mitra (who shot interiors), and broke barriers in the male-dominated Chinese film industry. M+ Restored, an initiative of the eponymous Hong Kong museum, made use of two 35mm release prints for their restoration, allowing T’ang’s visual style, which utilizes natural light, zooms, and superimpositions, among a myriad of techniques, to reach audiences once again.

Queen Kelly (Erich von Stroheim, 1929)

Decades in the making, Milestone Films and its co-founder Dennis Doros’s detailed reconstruction of von Stroheim’s never-finished penultimate film—about the misadventures of a convent girl—brings the decadence of the original script to the screen in an inspiring fashion, utilizing new research and recently discovered materials.

Forty Deuce (Paul Morrissey, 1982)

While the exhibited print was not a traditional restoration, the Metrograph theater, in collaboration with the Paul Morrissey Films Trust and Vinegar Syndrome, presented a 35mm screening of Morrissey’s gritty New York drama, which, to quote the dearly departed Gary Indiana, has “pacing that completely takes your mind off your stomach.” Two different film prints of varying quality were blended into one viewable print, giving audiences the rare opportunity to see the movie in its original and intended format.

article_text:
Fabrice Vallon, photographer between Paris and Milos, Fabrice Vallon captures fragments of life. Portraits volés captures the fragile instant of a passing face. Happy Capsules preserves the light of the Aegean Sea within photographs.

«I steal faces as if they were landscapes, and landscapes as if they were emotions.»

In 2026, Regards Volés captures the essence of travel through the stolen gaze of an explorer. The eyes, reflecting lived emotions and experiences, are framed by an iconic destination. Every detail—from vibrant colours to subtle expressions—evokes wonder and discovery.

These photographs embody not only a place, but also the love, energy, madness, memories and stories carried by every traveller: a dreamlike sublimation of imagination. In this series, the gaze—and the act of listening itself—becomes a landscape. A fragment of humanity seized in a fleeting instant, almost clandestinely, around a street corner, in a harbour or beneath an unexpected light.

The portrait is no longer simply a face: it becomes an open doorway to elsewhere. Landscapes, cities and atmospheres merge like layered memories. Each image forms an intimate cartography of travel, where identity dissolves into the world it encounters. Portraits volés are sensitive traces: suspended moments between reality and imagination, where the traveller’s gaze becomes the mirror of a dream in motion.

These stolen gazes portray a living world—the world that inspires the artist, gives him life, and ultimately becomes his own.

Happy Capsules – Milos

Created on the island of Milos, the Happy Capsules series explores a visual language at the crossroads of photography and sculpture. Since 2010, Fabrice Vallon has drawn inspiration from this mineral and sensual landscape, shaping a singular artistic language forged by light, wind and energy.

Carried by the Meltem—the wind of the Eastern Mediterranean, once regarded in Antiquity as a gift from Zeus—these works capture a delicate balance between tension and serenity, natural force and surrender to dreams.

These photographs function as capsules of happiness and freedom, fragments of summer and the sea. Inspired by the spectacular landscapes of Sarakiniko, they reveal a secret, colourful vision of intoxicating places where matter becomes emotion, inviting the viewer into a captivating space between dream and reality.

Their almost sculptural forms appear to emerge from light itself, creating vibrant volumes that are both organic and abstract. At the boundary between image and matter, each photograph becomes a sensory capsule—a concentrated vision of summer, sea and freedom.

Fabrice Vallon – Exhibition Schedule & Artist Presence

November 7 – Opening Day | 11:00 AM – 6:00 PM

November 8 – Saint Hubert’s Mass at 11:00 AM, followed by a guided visit of the exhibition.

November 14 – Artist present | 11:00 AM – 6:00 PM

November 21 – Come and Have Your Portrait Stolen! | 11:00 AM – 6:00 PM

November 28 – Closing Day | 11:00 AM – 6:00 PM

Saint-Eustache Church, Salle des Colonnes Paris, November 7 – November 28, 2026 The exhibition is open during church visiting hours.

article_text:
Museum closures are expected to take place across Paris on Saturday, in anticipation of planned protests, reports Le Figaro .

The Louvre, Musée d’Orsay, Musée de l’Orangerie, Picasso Museum, and the Grand Palais’s exhibition spaces will all close their doors on Saturday. The news follows the cancelation of Art Basel Paris over the weekend, which is held at the Grand Palais. In a statement on Friday, the French Ministry of Culture said that all establishments must ensure “the safety of visitors, the protection of agents and the preservation of works.” All national and public museums are being urged to shut their doors; meanwhile, many shops have started boarding up their windows in case of a second round of looting, following last weekend’s civil unrest in the wake of mostly peaceful protests held across France, in response to social and economic inequality amid a rising cost of living.

To maintain order across the country, French President Emmanuel Macron announced that only protests organized by unions are authorized on Saturday, with partial curfews put in place in several cities. According to the Associated Press , around 70,000 law enforcement officers will be deployed across the country on Saturday and protests in cities including Lyon, Nice, and Montpellier have been banned for security reasons. Marches are still expected to take place in Paris and Marseille.

On Friday, interior minister Laurent Nunez told reporters that the government will be “uncompromising with rioters, looters and all those who commit acts of violence.” He added that the authorities had located numerous online calls from hard-left groups encouraging attacks and urging activists to target public buildings. “We are not talking about a nice, friendly demonstration. We are ready for tomorrow. We will be extremely vigilant, extremely firm, and we will let absolutely nothing pass,” said Nunez.

In response to last weekend’s violence, President Macron said, “We witnessed both political and even seditious acts carried out by organised ultra-left groups aiming to bring down the Republic – acts that these groups themselves openly claim, characterised by extreme, intense violence.”

On Thursday, ARTnews was the first to report that Fondation Louis Vuitton would close its doors ahead of the planned protest on Saturday.

article_text:
Indian filmmaker Sanjay Gupta , whose credits include the crime thriller “ Kaante ,” the gangster saga “Shootout at Wadala” and the Hrithik Roshan-starring “Kaabil,” has died following a fall at his Mumbai residence on Oct. 30. He was 59, according to the Press Trust of India .

Director Milap Zaveri, a longtime friend of Gupta who worked on the dialogue for “Kaante,” confirmed the death to PTI. “It is true that he passed away. He fell and hit his head,” Zaveri said.

Police in Mumbai’s Versova neighborhood have filed an accidental death report. Deputy Commissioner of Police Purushottam Karad told the Free Press Journal that members of Gupta’s family were sleeping when the incident occurred and became aware of it the following morning. “The family has not raised any suspicion or lodged a complaint,” Karad said.

Gupta was a prominent exponent of the glossy, action-driven Hindi-language crime thriller, bringing a visual sensibility heavily indebted to Hollywood to an industry traditionally dominated by melodrama and musicals. His career behind the camera began with “Aatish: Feel the Fire” in 1994, featuring Sanjay Dutt and Aditya Pancholi. He subsequently directed “Ram Shastra,” “Jung” and “Khauff,” developing an enduring professional relationship with Dutt that extended across 10 films, including projects Gupta produced.

The filmmaker achieved one of his biggest successes with “Kaante” in 2002, assembling Amitabh Bachchan , Dutt, Suniel Shetty, Mahesh Manjrekar, Lucky Ali and Kumar Gaurav for a Los Angeles-set heist thriller about a group of criminals planning a bank robbery. The production was filming in the city when the terrorist attacks of Sept. 11, 2001, forced changes to its location schedule, as Gupta recounted in a Rediff interview the following year.

The film’s similarities to Quentin Tarantino ‘s “Reservoir Dogs” drew considerable attention, although Tarantino subsequently expressed admiration for “Kaante” in a 2007 interview covered by the Times of India . Gupta received a Filmfare nomination for best director.

Questions about the influence of international films followed Gupta throughout his career, and he made little secret of his willingness to draw inspiration from existing material. Responding to accusations of plagiarism in his 2002 Rediff interview, he said he would “beg, borrow and steal from any medium” in pursuit of a compelling story.

Several of his subsequent films reflected that philosophy. “Musafir” (2004) bore similarities to Oliver Stone’s “U Turn,” while the Dutt and John Abraham thriller “Zinda” (2006) attracted particular controversy over its resemblance to Park Chan-wook’s South Korean film “Oldboy.” The Korean production company Show East told Star News in November 2005 that it was considering legal remedies should the completed Hindi film prove substantially similar to the original. Gupta later directed “Jazbaa” (2015), an adaptation of the Korean thriller “Seven Days” that brought Aishwarya Rai Bachchan back to the screen.

Gupta also established himself as a producer through White Feather Films. The company’s credits included “Shootout at Lokhandwala” (2007), “Acid Factory,” “Pankh” and the anthology “Dus Kahaniyaan,” which Gupta also directed. He returned to the gangster genre with “Shootout at Wadala” (2013), a prequel to “Shootout at Lokhandwala” drawing on S. Hussain Zaidi’s nonfiction book “Dongri to Dubai.”

With “Kaabil” in 2017, Gupta directed Hrithik Roshan as a visually impaired man pursuing vengeance, in a film produced by Rakesh Roshan. His later work included the crime drama “Mumbai Saga” (2021), a T-Series co-production whose theatrical prospects were affected by a renewed surge in COVID-19 infections. His producing credits also extended to “Visfot” (2024), a Hindi adaptation of the Venezuelan thriller “Rock, Paper, Scissors.”

Colleagues remembered Gupta’s contributions to the industry’s visual and promotional vocabulary. “Raees” director Rahul Dholakia described him on X as a stylish filmmaker and “maybe the first to present trailers and cut promos to pitch the film idea to actors and distributors.”

Director Kunal Kohli, whose films include “Fanaa,” recalled a conversation with Gupta only a few weeks before his death, as well as their time together as members of an awards jury. “You had many more films and many years to go,” Kohli wrote .

Dutt posted : “Gupts, my brother. I still cannot believe that you are gone. We have shared so much together, so many memories and so many years of friendship. You have always been family to me, and that will never change. I will miss you, our conversations and all the times we spent together.”

Sound designer Resul Pookutty, Oscar winner for “Slumdog Millionaire,” wrote : “What a terrible and shocking news for me personally and our friends and family. 25 Years of working together. I’m not able to process this… we will miss you, one of the sanest voices from mainstream Hindi cinema… May your soul rest in eternal peace.”

Beyond filmmaking, Gupta maintained an active presence on X, frequently offering pointed commentary on the Hindi film industry’s creative and commercial direction. He had also begun discussing a possible return to one of his best-known properties. Following the resolution of a dispute involving White Feather Films and Pritish Nandy Communications over “Kaante,” Gupta revealed on the “InControversial” podcast earlier this year that he had developed the foundations of a sequel.

He said the story for “Kaante 2” had been worked out “at a very base level” and that he intended to begin writing the screenplay.

Gupta is survived by his wife and two children.

article_text:
ITSLIQUID Group is opening the official call for the 26th edition of VENICE INTERNATIONAL ART FAIR 2026. Hosted in the prestigious 16th-century Palazzo Albrizzi-Capello, the exhibition runs from December 04 to December 18, 2026, during Venice’s Christmas season, with the city dressed in its winter lights: a uniquely evocative stage for artists to present their work in the heart of the city.

VENICE ART FAIR invites artists to explore the dialogue between body, identity, and space within contemporary society. Through its two main sections, LIQUID ROOMS and FUTURE LANDSCAPES, the exhibition offers a unique opportunity to present works that challenge perception and open new perspectives.

Venice becomes the meeting point between these two visions, an invitation for artists to bring their own language into this dialogue, and to shape, through their work, new ways of perceiving reality. Since 2001, ITSLIQUID Group has organised over 350 international events, engaging more than 10,000 artists across over 60 global venues. Its initiatives have featured prestigious museums, galleries and private foundations. Thanks to its partnership with Sedition, ITSLIQUID has presented masters such as Bill Viola and Refik Anadol, offering high-level opportunities for young, mid-career, and renowned artists.

article_text:
Warner Bros. isn’t the only Los Angeles institution getting absorbed into Skydance this month. The Bay Theatre in Pacific Palisades, which was formerly operated by Netflix and before that by Cinepolis, will be taken over by Paramount Pictures with San Diego’s The Lot handling operations. The opening is planned for later this year.

The Bay Theatre has been closed since the wildfires damaged much of the upscale Los Angeles community in January 2025. The five-screen multiplex is located in Rick Caruso’s Palisades Village shopping area, which reopened in August after extensive remediation and repairs due to the fires. The theater’s vintage-looking sign is a nod to the community’s historic Bay Theatre, which stood nearby on Sunset Boulevard until closing in 1978.

Related Stories

‘Blade Runner 2099’ Trailer: Michelle Yeoh, Hunter Schafer Are Fugitives in Amazon Limited Series

Nicolas Cage Says He’s ‘Probably Not’ Working With Amazon Again After Refusing to Sign AI Waiver for ‘Spider-Noir,' Teases Joining 'True Detective'

Caruso made the deal with Paramount to showcase first-run theatrical releases, classic films, events and special programming. The theater offers luxurious seating, state-of-the-art sound and projection, in-theater dining and signature cocktails.

“The theater will also serve as a dynamic entertainment destination that extends the theatrical experience beyond the screen, through experiential activations and immersive theatrical moments,” the companies said in a statement.

David Ellison , chairman and CEO of Skydance, said in a statement, “Together with Caruso, we are proud to help bring the Bay back to life as a place for the Pacific Palisades community to gather around the shared experience of cinema. This theater has always meant more than movies alone — it’s woven into the fabric of this neighborhood, and helping restore it is a privilege. We’re inspired by the resilience of Pacific Palisades residents, and we’re honored to help support this community’s comeback.”

Caruso said, “Paramount is one of the world’s leading entertainment studios, with an extraordinary legacy of cinematic storytelling and, importantly, a deep commitment to the City of Los Angeles and to the future of the theatrical experience. Together, we see an opportunity to bring that to the Bay with the care, design and hospitality we’re known for, so that every visit feels special. The Bay has always been at the heart of the Palisades, and its return is one of the most meaningful signs yet that this community, following the reopening of the Palisades Village this summer, is coming back stronger than ever. David Ellison and I have a shared ambition to make it one of Los Angeles’ premier moviegoing destinations. I am grateful for David’s leadership and commitment to Los Angeles and the entertainment industry.”

editorial_title_zh: 胡安·马丁内斯：“我曾经居住的地方，如今居住在我体内”
editorial_excerpt_zh: 旅居伦敦的波多黎各艺术家胡安·马丁内斯（Jun Martínez）深入思考了距离、归属感，以及在其绘画中交织的美与暴力的张力。在这场对话中，他探讨了其故乡的风景如何延续至他的创作实践中，并分享了全新的……
editorial_blocks_json: [{"type": "heading", "text": "多年来，胡安·马丁内斯（1992年生于巴亚蒙）一直在户外作画，沉浸在他故乡波多黎各的自然环境中，密切关注着那里的光线、声音，以及他与这片土地建立起的亲密联系。自从大约三年前定居伦敦以来，这一切并未消失，也没有在其表现形式中耗尽。他曾经面对的风景开始以另一种方式栖居于他体内，经过了回忆以及远离加勒比海日常生活的体验的过滤。", "translated": true}, {"type": "heading", "text": "今年年中，他在塞西莉亚布伦森项目空间（Cecilia Brunson Projects）举办了首场个展“中心唯有宁静”（At the centre there is a stillness），展出了他在伦敦根据对波多黎各自然环境的眷恋创作的绘画。在这些作品中，色彩依然保留着某种加勒比海的浓烈，但如今它呼应的是另一种光线；而物质与笔触则展现了美与暴力之间的这种共生关系，正是这种关系定义了他对风景的理解。", "translated": true}, {"type": "heading", "text": "胡安·马丁内斯正经历着作品国际流通日益增加的阶段。他即将携手这家伦敦画廊参加弗里兹伦敦艺博会（Frieze London），并正与策展人莎拉·赫曼（Sarah Hermann）合作，在多米尼加共和国筹备一个新的机构项目。这种地理上的拓展也改变了他的绘画方式。", "translated": true}, {"type": "heading", "text": "在这次对话中，马丁内斯谈到了他如今进行绘画的立足点，以及他的作品中开始出现的新问题，其中包括一项日益深入的研究，关注加勒比海的本土植被，以及那些来到这些领土并已在其中归化的物种。", "translated": true}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://artishockrevista.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/Jun-Martinez-en-su-studio-2023.-Foto-Raquel-Perez-Puig.jpg", "alt": "", "caption": "在工作室中的胡安·马丁内斯（2023年）。摄影：拉克尔·佩雷斯·普伊格（Raquel Perez Puig）", "credit": "Artishock", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "在你的绘画中，风景、记忆与身体体验交织在一起。你会如何描述你今天进行创作的立足点？自从定居伦敦以来，你是否觉得你与风景的关系发生了变化？", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "在我艺术实践最初的八年里，我的作品主要与我所居住的地方有关。尤其是我是如何将这个地方理解为同伴的，也就是说，几乎是从一种将地方拟人化的角度出发。我给自己设定了任务，去理解那些指导我接近土地、接近我祖国土地的伦理，将其视为一个有生命的实体。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "今天，在伦敦，同时忠实于我来此之前培养的绘画岁月，我觉得我越来越深刻地体会到：我曾经居住过的地方如今是如何居住在我体内的；它是如何在我的气质、我的思维方式、我的心理、我的灵性以及我的身体内部开辟出一个空间的。它甚至存在于我应对这座城市、或是应对气候的方式中——作为一个来自波多黎各的人。我想，现在的我的绘画对这两种可能性敞开了大门：一种是外部空间，即土地与风景意义上的空间；另一种则是内部空间。从这里出发，通往其他解读的门扉被打开了，并实现了对历史、自然、政治、生态等参考资料的更高程度的整合。", "translated": true}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://artishockrevista.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/Jose-Jun-Martinez-At-the-centre-there-is-a-stillness.jpg", "alt": "", "caption": Brunson Projects）", "credit": "Artishock", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "你对色彩的使用非常独特，它唤起了一种丰沛与蓬勃之感，而在这种浓烈之余，我们还能看到某些唤起暴力与冲突状态的笔触。你是如何在同一幅画作中处理这种表面上相互矛盾的状态的共存的？", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "我经常说，我对绘画的理解源于这样一个地方：我栖居在美与暴力、赞美与哀悼、庆祝与抗议之间的张力之中。这与我从风景和土地中学到的东西有关——因为我在其中直接度过了大量时间作画，沉浸在风景之中——也与我对加勒比海光线和色彩的关系有关。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "既然我不再居住在波多黎各群岛，这种色彩也随之发生了转变。也许过去我更直接地回应我在那里接收到的光线，而现在我回应的是我在伦敦接收到的光线，以及一种通过色彩的强度、通过那些或许看起来更具合成感或人工感的色彩来补偿它的需求。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "但这不仅关乎色彩。它同样存在于质感、媒介的施用方式以及我用来作画的各种材料中。这其中有很大一部分与手势以及绘画本身的物质性息息相关。这里面有很多暴力，而且在某种程度上，这也是对风景不幸地从我们自身以及那些不断剥削它的系统中遭受的暴力的一种疏导。归根结底，一切都源于一种需求：通过色彩、物质和手势，去沟通并赋予那些在风景出现或缺席时涌现的感受以意义。", "translated": true}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://artishockrevista.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/Jun-Martinez-en-Museo-de-San-Juan.jpg", "alt": "", "caption": "展览“花之兄弟：胡安·马丁内斯作品中的自然与情感”（Hermano de las flores: naturaleza y afectos en la obra de Jun Martínez）现场图，圣胡安博物馆，波多黎各，2026年。艺术家供图", "credit": "Artishock", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "事实上，你作品中的风景受到了历史以及我们居住和改造一个地方的方式的影响。今天你如何看待波多黎各风景中这种历史和政治的维度？面对那些其他语言或许会以不同方式处理的暴力，绘画能够做些什么？", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "我认为在创作时我遇到的主要挑战之一，是如何将我对绘画的方法与对自然环境遭受暴力的紧迫性和现实性的清醒认识调和起来——这种暴力尤其发生在波多黎各，但也发生在整个地球层面。以及如何通过拥抱这种关切将其融入我的作品，而不是站在标语、小册子或插图的立场，而是尊重我将绘画理解为一种关于物质性、对材料的操纵以及探索该材料可能性的工作，而不仅仅是创作一幅图像。", "translated": true}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://artishockrevista.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/Jose-Jun-Martinez-3.jpg", "alt": "", "caption": "", "credit": "Artishock", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "胡·马丁内斯，《论受改造的土地与荒废的草场（加勒比白橡树）I-III》，2026年。亚麻布油画，五联画。每幅：180 x 120 cm；总计：180 x 600 cm。鸣谢：塞西莉亚·布鲁森项目空间。展出于伦敦弗里兹艺博园，摄政公园，伦敦，2026年10月14日至18日。", "translated": true}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://artishockrevista.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/Jose-Jun-Martinez-2.jpg", "alt": "", "caption": "", "credit": "Artishock", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "胡·马丁内斯，《论受改造的土地与荒废的草场（加勒比白橡树）[局部]》，2026年。亚麻布油画，五联画。每幅：180 x 120 cm；总计：180 x 600 cm。鸣谢：塞西莉亚·布鲁森项目空间。展出于伦敦弗里兹艺博园，摄政公园，伦敦，2026年10月14日至18日。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "在伦敦弗里兹艺博会塞西莉亚·布鲁森项目空间展位的中心，将是一件以白橡树（Tabebuia heterophylla）为核心的五联画。这种树原产于波多黎各，以其呈粉色和白色调的壮观花冠而闻名，既是主题又是象征，其再造林的能力构成了生存与新生的象征。", "links": [{"text": "Frieze London", "url": "https://www.frieze.com/fairs/frieze-london/galleries"}], "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "马丁内斯将加勒比地区脆弱的美丽与生物多样性同其生态系统所承受的压力进行对照，白橡树由此成为一种将风景理解为活档案馆的方式。对这位艺术家而言，这种张力提供了一种具再生性的方案。风景既非被动，也非任由外部行为摆布。它是积极的、有生命的且能够自我更新的。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "从一个过去和现在依然深深打上与美国关系烙印的岛屿出发，马丁内斯借助自然世界的韧性作为重新想象地方的一种方式。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "你的作品目前正迎来日益广泛的国际流通，从你在波多黎各和墨西哥的展览，到伦敦以及即将到来的、与塞西莉亚·布鲁森项目空间合作的弗里兹艺博会。你如何看待从你作为波多黎各和加勒比艺术家的立场出发的这段历程？当这些与特定经验紧密相连的绘画在其他语境中被观看时，你希望发生什么？", "links": [{"text": "Cecilia Brunson Projects", "url": "https://www.ceciliabrunsonprojects.com/"}], "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "我无法想象以除我的经验与我所知之事的诚实之外的其他方式来创作我的作品。是的，我是一位波多黎各画家，现常驻伦敦。我并没有专画波多黎各风景，因为我也曾在其他地方画画，比如美国北部、加那利群岛和中美洲，并且根据我在那里所见所历创作了作品。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "今天，我所能呈现的，是一件诞生于从距离中思考自身地方的复杂性，同时也诞生于对其他亲近关系的发现中的作品。例如，我不排除通过绘画来探讨我目前居住的地方的可能性。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": article_text:
Durante años, Jun Martínez (Bayamón, 1992) pintó al aire libre, inmerso en los entornos naturales de su natal Puerto Rico, atento a su luz, sus sonidos y al vínculo íntimo que había construido con la tierra. Desde que se instaló en Londres, hace aproximadamente tres años, eso no desapareció, ni se agota en su representación. El paisaje que antes tenía delante comenzó a habitarlo de otra manera, filtrado por los recuerdos y la experiencia cotidiana de vivir lejos del Caribe.

A mediados de este año, presentó At the centre there is a stillness , su primera exposición individual con Cecilia Brunson Projects, donde reunió pinturas realizadas en Londres a partir del apego que mantiene con el entorno natural puertorriqueño. En ellas, el color conserva algo de la intensidad caribeña, pero responde ahora a otra luz, mientras que la materia y el gesto muestran esa convivencia entre belleza y violencia que define su concepción del paisaje.

Jun Martínez experimenta una etapa de creciente circulación internacional. Próximamente participará en la feria Frieze London con la galería londinense y prepara un nuevo proyecto institucional en República Dominicana junto a la curadora Sarah Hermann. Esta expansión geográfica también transforma su manera de pintar.

En esta conversación, Martínez habla de lugar desde el que está pintando hoy y de las nuevas preguntas que empiezan a aparecer en su trabajo, entre ellas una investigación cada vez más atenta a la vegetación nativa del Caribe y a las especies que han llegado a sus territorios y se han naturalizado en ellos.

En tu pintura convergen paisaje, memoria y experiencia corporal. ¿Cómo describirías el lugar desde el que estás pintando hoy? ¿Sientes que tu relación con el paisaje ha cambiado desde que te instalaste en Londres?

Durante los primeros ocho años de mi práctica artística, mi trabajo tenía que ver principalmente con el lugar que habitaba. Especialmente con cómo entendía ese lugar como prójimo, es decir, casi desde una personificación del lugar. Me daba a la tarea de entender las éticas que guiaban mi acercamiento a la tierra, y a la tierra de mi país, como un ente vivo.

Hoy, desde Londres, y manteniéndome fiel a los años de pintura que desarrollé antes de llegar aquí, creo que cada vez aprendo más sobre cómo ese lugar que antes yo habitaba ahora habita en mí; cómo fue haciéndose un lugar dentro de mi idiosincrasia, de mi manera de pensar, de mi psicología, de mi espiritualidad y también de mi cuerpo. Está presente incluso en las maneras en las que reacciono a la ciudad, viniendo de Puerto Rico, o al clima. Creo que ahora mi pintura se abre a esas dos posibilidades: la del espacio exterior, en el sentido de la tierra y del paisaje, y también la del espacio interior. Desde ahí se abren puertas a otras lecturas y a una mayor integración de referencias históricas, naturales, políticas, ecológicas, etcétera.

Tu uso del color es muy particular, ya que despierta una sensación de exuberancia y vitalidad, y junto a esa intensidad vemos también trazos que evocan ciertos estados de violencia y conflicto. ¿Cómo trabajas esa convivencia de estados aparentemente contradictorios en una misma pintura?

Yo digo mucho que mi entendimiento de la pintura parte de un lugar donde habito las tensiones entre la belleza y la violencia, la alabanza y el lamento, la celebración y la protesta. Eso tiene que ver con lo que he aprendido del paisaje y de la tierra al haber pasado tanto tiempo pintando directamente en ella, inmerso en el paisaje, y también con mi relación con la luz caribeña y el color.

Ese color se ha transformado ahora que ya no estoy viviendo en el archipiélago de Puerto Rico. Quizás antes reaccionaba más directamente a la luz que recibía allá, mientras que ahora reacciono a la luz que recibo en Londres y a una necesidad de compensarla a través de intensidades de color, con colores que quizás parecen más sintéticos o artificiales.

Pero no se trata solamente del color. También está en las texturas, en la manera de aplicar el medio y en los distintos materiales que utilizo para pintar. Hay algo que tiene mucho que ver con el gesto y con la fisicalidad misma de pintar. Hay mucha violencia ahí, y de alguna manera es también una canalización de la violencia que el paisaje recibe de nosotros mismos, lamentablemente, y de los sistemas que continuamente lo explotan. Al final del día, todo parte de una necesidad de comunicar y de darle sentido, a través del color, de la materia y del gesto, a esas sensaciones que surgen ante la presencia o la ausencia del paisaje.

De hecho, el paisaje en tu obra está influido por la historia y por las formas en que habitamos y transformamos un lugar. ¿Cómo piensas hoy esa dimensión histórica y política del paisaje puertorriqueño? ¿Qué puede hacer la pintura frente a esas violencias que otros lenguajes quizá abordan de otra manera?

Creo que uno de los desafíos principales que encuentro al hacer mi obra es cómo reconciliar mi acercamiento a la pintura con la conciencia de la urgencia y la actualidad de las violencias hacia el paisaje, particularmente en Puerto Rico, pero también a nivel del planeta completo. Y cómo, abrazando esa preocupación, la integro en mi obra, no desde un lugar de pancarta, panfleto o ilustración, sino respetando mi entendimiento de la pintura como un trabajo de materialidad, de la manipulación de un material y de la exploración de las posibilidades de este material, más allá de la realización de una imagen.

Jun Martínez, Sobre tierras alteradas y pastizales abandonados (Roble Blanco del Caribe) I-III , 2026. Óleo sobre lino, pentáptico. Cada uno: 180 x 120 cm; Total: 180 x 600 cm. Cortesía: Cecilia Brunson Projects. Presentada en Frieze London, The Regent’s Park, Londres, 14 – 18 octubre, 2026.

Jun Martínez, Sobre tierras alteradas y pastizales abandonados (Roble Blanco del Caribe) [detalle], 2026. Óleo sobre lino, pentáptico. Cada uno: 180 x 120 cm; Total: 180 x 600 cm. Cortesía: Cecilia Brunson Projects. Presentada en Frieze London, The Regent’s Park, Londres, 14 – 18 octubre, 2026.

En el centro del stand de Cecilia Brunson Projects en Frieze London se encontrará un pentáptico centrado en el roble blanco ( Tabebuia heterophylla ). Originario de Puerto Rico y famoso por su espectacular copa en flor de tonos rosados y blancos, el árbol funge tanto de tema como de símbolo, y su capacidad de reforestación se erige como un emblema de supervivencia y renovación.

Martínez contrapone la frágil belleza y la biodiversidad del Caribe a las presiones que se ejercen sobre sus ecosistemas, y el roble blanco se convierte en una forma de entender el paisaje como un archivo vivo. Para el artista, esta tensión ofrece una propuesta regenerativa. El paisaje no es pasivo ni está sujeto a acciones externas. Es activo, vivo y capaz de renovarse.

Desde una isla cuyo pasado y presente siguen profundamente marcados por su relación con Estados Unidos, Martínez recurre a la resiliencia del mundo natural como una forma de reimaginar el lugar.

Tu obra está teniendo ahora una circulación internacional cada vez mayor, desde tus exposiciones en Puerto Rico y México, hasta Londres y próximamente Frieze, con Cecilia Brunson Projects . ¿Cómo piensas ese recorrido desde tu lugar como artista puertorriqueño y caribeño? ¿Qué te interesa que ocurra cuando estas pinturas, tan vinculadas a una experiencia específica, sean vistas desde otros contextos?

No imagino otra manera de hacer mi trabajo que no sea desde la honestidad de mi experiencia y de lo que conozco. Sí, soy un pintor puertorriqueño, hoy radicado en Londres. No he pintado exclusivamente paisajes puertorriqueños, porque he pintado en otros lugares, como el norte de los Estados Unidos, las Islas Canarias y Centroamérica, y he hecho obra a partir de lo que he visto y vivido allí.

Hoy, lo que puedo ofrecer es una obra que nace de la complejidad de pensar el lugar propio desde la distancia, pero también desde el descubrimiento de otras cercanías. No me cierro, por ejemplo, a la posibilidad de abordar, desde la pintura, el lugar donde estoy viviendo ahora.

Históricamente, los artistas puertorriqueños, y hablo de los puertorriqueños porque es la historia que conozco, han salido del archipiélago, ya sea para formarse o para participar de las escenas del arte en otras metrópolis y otros países. Muchas de nuestras maestras y maestros, quienes sentaron las bases de nuestra herencia artística, han tenido también esos recorridos.

En mi caso escogí Londres, que quizás no es uno de los destinos más comunes para los artistas puertorriqueños, aunque sí reconozco a maestros y colegas que me han precedido en su paso por esta ciudad, cuyo trabajo admiro. Estar aquí me está abriendo puertas, sobre todo para participar de la conversación del arte contemporáneo desde lo que he recibido en mi formación en Puerto Rico y desde las realidades que me han formado. Pero también siento que la distancia me ha permitido afianzarme como artista puertorriqueño en mis propios términos, quizás con menos condicionamientos externos de los que pienso que hubiera recibido de haberme relocalizado en alguna ciudad de los Estados Unidos, por todas las implicaciones particulares que tiene ser un artista puertorriqueño allí. No es una realidad que quiera negar ni de la que quiera desvincularme, pero sí me interesaba tomar cierta distancia de esa influencia y de algunas de las predeterminaciones que pueden acompañarla. Estar en Londres me provoca mirar desde otros ángulos mi lugar de origen, mi relación con el Caribe y mi propia práctica.

Próximamente presentarás tu trabajo en República Dominicana. ¿Qué puedes adelantarnos sobre este proyecto y qué te interesa poner en juego en ese contexto caribeño?

El trabajo para República Dominicana aún está en desarrollo, pero puedo adelantar que estará caracterizado por el sentimiento, la historia y el sueño de hermandad antillana entre mi país y el que me recibe, siempre encarnado en la experiencia de la tierra. Será, además, un proyecto institucional que estamos trabajando junto a la curadora Sarah Hermann.

Mirando hacia adelante, ¿qué preguntas están ocupando actualmente tu pintura? ¿Sientes que algo está comenzando a abrir una nueva etapa en tu trabajo?

Creo que mi trabajo cada vez más se convierte en el lugar que necesito, en el espacio donde puedo albergar reflexiones y referencias tanto de mi país como de otros contextos que he ido recibiendo. No solo en el desarrollo de los elementos pictóricos sino en la integración de otras disciplinas como la historia, la historia del arte, la literatura, la teología y la ecología.

Particularmente, en el trabajo más reciente he comenzado a prestar más atención a aspectos científicos específicos de la vegetación que habita mis composiciones. Estoy estudiando acerca de los árboles nativos de Puerto Rico y el Caribe, o cómo llegaron otras especies que no son nativas pero que con el tiempo se han naturalizado. Es algo cada vez más presente en mi proceso y que entiendo también como una manera de mantenerme cercano a aquello que, de alguna forma, estoy representando o evocando en mis pinturas.
excerpt_original: Desde Londres, el artista puertorriqueño Jun Martínez reflexiona sobre la distancia, la pertenencia y las tensiones entre belleza y violencia que atraviesan su pintura. En esta conversación, aborda cómo el paisaje de su isla natal persiste en su práctica y comparte las nuevas…

article_text:
[Editor’s note: This review was originally published on January 28, 2026 at the 2026 Sundance Film Festival. Sony Pictures Classics will release the film in theaters on Friday, October 23.]

It’s become commonplace in recent years: movies set in New York , telling distinctly New York stories, yet shot entirely somewhere else like Ireland. Given Hollywood’s economic slowdown, an indie production can be forgiven for doing whatever it takes to get a film made. Still, many films no longer seem interested in even attempting to suspend disbelief about place.

Which makes ” The Only Living Pickpocket in New York ” feel like a minor miracle and a welcome update to the New York crime movie genre. Writer/director Noah Segan shoots not only in Manhattan, but across the city’s outer boroughs like the Bronx, Queens, and Brooklyn, capturing a New York that feels authentic rather than postcard-ready. The film’s most satisfying image arrives late: a 360 view of the harbor skyline seen not from lower Manhattan but from the murky New Jersey shoreline, lensed by Sam Levy with bracing clarity. Though the credits list a Los Angeles unit, its scenes disappear seamlessly into the world of the film.

This Sundance-premiering indie drama stars John Turturro in a controlled, assured performance as Harry Lehman, an old-school pickpocket shaped by decades on New York’s streets. He’s a con man guided by a code. A funk-inflected score — think ”The Payback”-era James Brown — may land a bit heavy-handed, but it effectively establishes a tone of Big Apple toughness that moves into a rhythm measured in city blocks and subway stops.

Segan, a protégé of Rian Johnson whose T-Street banner produced the microbudget film along with MRC, delivers a script that moves with confidence and precision. The visual language toggles purposefully between wide shots and tight close-ups, mirroring Harry’s ability to survey a room and zero in on his take with surgical precision. Before the opening credits, Harry lifts a wallet from a Wall Street guy on the subway — who only notices the loss once he’s seated at a white-tablecloth lunch downtown.

Harry wears the same gray tweed trench coat and polished brown leather oxfords throughout the film. The coat’s hidden inside pocket — a key tool of the trade — becomes a kind of uniform, like that of a janitor or a waitress — neat, understated and designed to disappear. But Turturro doesn’t rely on wardrobe or makeup to sell the character. Harry is a man of few words, so the performance hinges on his physical control and interiority. Turturro delivers both. His pickpocket research is evident — he practiced by lifting from cast and crew — and his movements register with quiet confidence. Harry doesn’t flare up when threatened; he turns inward, calculates, and seizes upon his next move chameleonlike.

Petty theft in Harry’s world follows strict rules: analogue only. No credit cards. No fraud. Just cash and pawnable items destined for resale. When Harry brings his take to Ben, a pawnshop dealer played with steady warmth by Steve Buscemi, he explains that his Wall Street mark carried “all platinum cards” but no cash. The problem is immediately clear: Harry’s expertise hasn’t vanished, but its value has shrunk in a consumer economy dominated by Apple Pay and swipe-lock security.

That friction between analogue and digital fuels one of the film’s central tensions and produces its best humor. In one scene, Harry hands Ben an external data card to load onto Ben’s ancient, 40-pound desktop computer. The machine can’t even read it, yet still manages to alert the card’s owner. “That’s how they get ya,” Harry and Ben mutter, realizing the system demands an upgrade. Later, Harry refers to a corrupted file as having “an illness,” prompting a Gen-Z character to translate: he actually meant virus.

The ensemble cast gives the film its emotional weight. Tatiana Maslany — unrecognizable, as usual — leaves a devastating impression as Harry’s estranged daughter. Harry’s wife Rosie, unable to walk or speak and requiring constant care, is rendered with extraordinary sensitivity. Through the smallest facial shifts and precise physical stillness, the actor conveys a full inner life. A brief but piercing detail completes the portrait: Rosie’s once high-pitched voice, preserved on an answering machine Harry refuses to discard, offers a glimpse of the woman she once was. Lori Tan Chinn charms as a cantankerous Chinatown grandmother, while Jamie Lee Curtis makes a memorable meal of her single scene as a mob boss.

The film’s boldest choice may be what it refuses to show. No guns are waved. No bodies pile up. Violence exists as pressure rather than spectacle. When Harry discovers a gun in one of his hauls, he tosses it into the trash. When Ben’s shop windows are smashed, we find him stunned on the floor, clutching a bat. ”The Only Living Pickpocket in New York” proves that crime stories don’t need bloodshed and gratuitous violence to land with force.

What emerges is a New York crime drama attuned to the present moment, one that makes space for aging lifers like Harry and Ben alongside younger characters born bluetooth enabled. Everyone struggles to remain in a city where rent keeps climbing and even five-generation families can’t hold onto their homes. The film treats New York itself as a character — not just Manhattan, and certainly not only the Upper East Side — moving with restraint and confidence, grounded in the primary source of its charm: real New Yorkers.

Crucially, the film avoids the trap of scolding younger generations or romanticizing the past. “I like that they don’t just get put on the shelf,” a woman sitting next to me at the Sundance premiere whispered as the credits rolled, phone already back in hand. She’s right. Harry adapts, relying on Ben’s Gen-Z relative (Victoria Moroles), a computer whiz who handles the digital transactions Harry would never be able to —or want to — master.

It’s impossible not to root for Harry and Ben: two flawed, aging men sustained by skills learned the hard way. They pick locks by feel, break into old cars with pennies, trade favors, maintain relationships, and above all, know how to “work,” as Harry puts it, actual human beings. Ultimately ”The Only Living Pickpocket in New York” shows us that old school and new school aren’t opposites. Like the city’s many seeming contradictions, they are meant to coexist.

Grade: A

“The Only Living Pickpocket in New York” premiered at the 2026 Sundance Film Festival.

article_text:
Films and events

Documentary Competition

Queer Edward II

This all-archival tour de force takes us behind the scenes of Derek Jarman’s Edward II, set against the backdrop of the anti-LGBTQIA+ legislation of 1980s Britain.

Screening dates and booking

Check which tickets are still available across the festival – and find out about extra ticket releases and standby queues .

Credits

Director-screenwriter Theo Rollason

UK 2026. 97min

Courtesy of Lightborn Films

Language English

Access information

Sunday 11 October 18:00

Audio description

Tuesday 13 October 20:45

Audio description

Descriptive subtitles

Sunday 18 October 19:00

Audio description

Descriptive subtitles

Find out about booking access tickets

Introduction

This all-archival tour de force takes us behind the scenes of Derek Jarman’s Edward II, set against the backdrop of the anti-LGBTQIA+ legislation of 1980s Britain. In 1991, Jarman started production on Edward II, just as queer life in the UK was under renewed threat from the British government. Seamus McGarvey captured all the drama on set in a previously unseen treasure trove of behind-the-scenes footage. Queer Edward II masterfully reanimates this archive as a vigorous and radical reflection on the power of art as protest.

Chloé Trayner

Content advice

Contains homophobic attitudes and language.

How to book

Tickets start from £10 for all screenings and events in London, with concessions available for many screenings. Booking information and ticket prices .

For non-Members we charge £1 per ticket for online and phone bookings, up to £3 per transaction. There’s no booking fee if you buy tickets at the box office.

If you’re aged 16 to 25, sign up for free to BFI 25 and Under for a chance to get £6 tickets (without booking fees) to all screenings and events, subject to availability.

Missed out?

More tickets may become available for these screenings before and during the festival. Find out about extra ticket releases and standby queues .

Our programmers recommend...

Act 3

The latest in Christine Molloy and Joe Lawlor’s series of cinematic essays is a rich and thought-provoking journey through ageing, legacy and the intersection between artistic and personal relationships.

Elsinore

Andrew Scott is a towering presence in this singular account of Ian Charleson’s life, capturing the moment when he faced his own mortality as he prepared to play Hamlet at the Royal National Theatre.

The Man I Love: Remembering the AIDS Crisis

This event gives space for remembrance and reflection on the legacy and lasting impact of the AIDS epidemic.

article_text:
Cine

Almas gemelas

Cristina Vales

Equals es una interesante propuesta de ciencia ficción que, aunque no logra convencer del todo, puede ser una buena alternativa a los grandes blockbusters.

La película Almas gemelas (2015) presenta una sociedad utópica en la cual las emociones son reprimidas desde el nacimiento para obtener un mejor rendimiento de sus ciudadanos. Todo cambia para el protagonista, Silas ( Nicholas Hoult ), cuando comienza a experimentar sentimientos que eventualmente lo llevan a enamorarse de Nia (Kristen Stewart), una chica que, como él, vive en la sombra ya que descubre que puede sentir. Ahora ambos deberán descubrir una manera de desafiar al sistema para poder estar juntos sin que la sociedad los castigue.

Desde sus inicios, la ciencia ficción ha buscado mostrar los problemas de la sociedad desde una manera metafórica. En la mayoría de los casos, y si se analiza a profundidad, se puede encontrar una crítica a la manera en la que vivimos o las consecuencias de continuar por el mismo camino –no es casualidad que nos parezca tan tétrico Black Mirror .

Esta introspección es lo que trata de lograr Almas gemelas , que explora la desensibilización de la sociedad ante las emociones humanas. Aquí lo único que vale es lo que uno puede aportar a un nivel práctico, algo así como lo que sucede en muchos ámbitos del mundo real.

El escenario alternativo planteado por Drake Doremus

La representación de un mundo desensibilizado, utilitario y totalmente pragmático, que tiene un lugar para las emociones, busca despertarnos ante el individualismo de nuestra sociedad. El impacto de qué podría pasar si seguimos por ese camino nos inquieta porque se siente cercano a lo que vivimos día con día.

Esto no sería posible sin la presencia de Hoult y Stewart, quienes logran crear empatía con la audiencia. Es grato verlos separarse de sus roles en cintas de alto presupuesto porque es algo que no esperamos de ellos. Pero, a pesar de contar con una sólida presencia protagónica, la película decae al tratar de abarcar más aspectos de la sociedad.

Sus buenos escenarios, gran diseño de producción, protagonistas interesantes y una premisa que resuena, no son suficientes para sostener un universo que no existe. Es decir, tiene un inicio sólido que involucra a la audiencia; sin embargo, la historia va perdiendo fuerza en cuanto las reglas del juego cambian. La razón es que este universo nunca queda lo suficientemente claro como para ser convincente. No logra la célebre “ suspension of disbelief ” (es decir, que «nos creamos» lo que estamos viendo) porque faltan aspectos clave dentro del guion que resultan en huecos de trama imposibles de ignorar.

Eta cinta no alcanza el nivel de otras de ciencia ficción cuyo propósito es la reflexión –los invitamos a ver Another Earth o Nunca me abandones . Sobre todo, por su guion que termina en un final abrupto. No obstante, es importante recalcar que sí es una propuesta distinta a lo que estamos acostumbrados a ver en cines. Se agradece que haya cineastas como Drake Doremus ( Like Crazy ) que quieren darle a la ciencia ficción una profundidad que va más allá de los gadgets y los universos utópicos agradables a la vista.

Cristina Vales Cristina Vales fue editora de Cine PREMIERE por casi tres años, sin embargo, su lado geek la ha mantenido cerca. Búsquenla si quieren hablar de Buffy la Caza Vampiros, libros y todo lo que tenga que ver con entretenimiento.
